claim: The budding yeast Stu2 in complex with the γ-tubulin receptor Spc72 nucleates microtubules in vitro without the small γ-tubulin complex (γ-TuSC).
source: Here, we show that the budding yeast Stu2 in complex with the γ-tubulin receptor Spc72 nucleates microtubules in vitro without the small γ-tubulin complex (γ-TuSC).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro experimental data presented in the manuscript showing MT nucleation by Spc72-Stu2 complex.

claim: Upon γ-TuSC addition, Stu2 facilitates Spc72–γ-TuSC interaction by binding to Spc72 and γ-TuSC.
source: Upon γ-TuSC addition, Stu2 facilitates Spc72–γ-TuSC interaction by binding to Spc72 and γ-TuSC.
evidence: This claim is supported by binding affinity measurements and pulldown experiments showing Stu2 binds both Spc72 and γ-TuSC.

claim: Stu2 together with Spc72–γ-TuSC increases microtubule nucleation in a process that is dependent on the TOG domains of Stu2.
source: Stu2 together with Spc72–γ-TuSC increases microtubule nucleation in a process that is dependent on the TOG domains of Stu2.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro MT nucleation assays comparing wildtype Stu2 with TOG domain mutants.

claim: Stu2 stabilizes Spc72–γ-TuSC at the minus end of cytoplasmic microtubules (cMTs).
source: Stu2 stabilizes Spc72–γ-TuSC at the minus end of cytoplasmic microtubules (cMTs)
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments showing γ-TuSC dissociation from cMT minus ends when Stu2 is removed.

claim: An in vivo assay indicates that cMT nucleation requires the TOG domains of Stu2.
source: an in vivo assay indicates that cMT nucleation requires the TOG domains of Stu2.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments showing impaired cMT nucleation in cells expressing Stu2 with mutated TOG domains.

claim: Upon γ-tubulin depletion, efficient cMT nucleation occurs away from the spindle pole body (SPB), which is dependent on Stu2.
source: Upon γ-tubulin depletion, we observed efficient cMT nucleation away from the spindle pole body (SPB), which was dependent on Stu2.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments showing cMT nucleation in the cytoplasm in Tub4-depleted cells that is abolished when Stu2 is also depleted.

claim: γ-TuSC restricts cMT assembly to the SPB.
source: Thus, γ-TuSC restricts cMT assembly to the SPB
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that γ-tubulin depletion leads to ectopic cMT nucleation away from the SPB.

claim: Stu2 nucleates cMTs together with γ-TuSC.
source: Stu2 nucleates cMTs together with γ-TuSC
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro and in vivo experiments showing enhanced MT nucleation when Stu2, Spc72, and γ-TuSC are present together.

claim: Stu2 stabilizes γ-TuSC at the cMT minus end.
source: Stu2 nucleates cMTs together with γ-TuSC and stabilizes γ-TuSC at the cMT minus end.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments showing γ-TuSC dissociation from cMT minus ends when Stu2 is removed.

claim: The γ-tubulin small complex (γ-TuSC) of budding yeast contains γ-tubulin Tub4, GCP2/Spc97 and GCP3/Spc98.
source: The γ-tubulin small complex (γ-TuSC) of budding yeast contains γ-tubulin Tub4, GCP2/Spc97 and GCP3/Spc98.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the composition of γ-TuSC in budding yeast.

claim: The γ-TuSC oligomerizes into a left-handed spiral upon interaction with the γ-tubulin receptor protein Spc110 at the nuclear side of the yeast spindle pole body (SPB).
source: The γ-TuSC oligomerizes into a left-handed spiral upon interaction with the γ-tubulin receptor protein Spc110 at the nuclear side of the yeast spindle pole body (SPB) (Geissler et al., 1996; Knop and Schiebel, 1997, 1998; Kollman et al., 2010; Nguyen et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that characterized γ-TuSC oligomerization.

claim: In human cells, the γ-TuSC, together with GCP4, GCP5 and GCP6, forms a stable γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC).
source: In human cells, the γ-TuSC, together with GCP4, GCP5 and GCP6, forms a stable γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) (Zheng et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the composition of γ-TuRC in human cells, supported by citation.

claim: Through the interaction of γ-tubulin with α/β-tubulin, the kinetic barrier of α/β-tubulin oligomerization is overcome and MT assembly is facilitated.
source: Through the interaction of γ-tubulin with α/β-tubulin, the kinetic barrier of α/β-tubulin oligomerization is overcome and MT assembly is facilitated (Kollman et al., 2011; Roostalu and Surrey, 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the mechanism of γ-tubulin-mediated MT nucleation, supported by citations.

claim: Stu2 belongs to a family of proteins that contain TOG (Tumour Overexpressed Gene) domains and function as MT polymerases.

evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the TOG domain protein family.

claim: TOG domain proteins localize to both the plus and the minus end of MTs.
source: They localize to both the plus and the minus end of MTs (Ayaz et al., 2012; Ayaz et al., 2014; Brouhard et al., 2008; Podolski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing localization of TOG domain proteins.

claim: The two TOG domains at the N-terminus of budding yeast Stu2 can directly bind α/β-tubulin.
source: The two TOG domains at the N-terminus of budding yeast Stu2 can directly bind α/β-tubulin.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Stu2 function, supported by citations.

source: Further on, Stu2 can be recruited to MTs via its C-terminal MT-binding site.

claim: The interaction of Stu2 with MTs recruits the α/β-tubulin heterodimer to the growing MT plus end, promoting MT polymerisation.

evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Stu2's mechanism of action, supported by citations.

claim: XMAP215 has the ability to interact with purified human γ-tubulin via its C-terminal MT-binding domain.

source: Importantly, the binding affinity of γ-TuSC to the truncated N-terminal construct of Spc110 (Spc110N, aa 1–220) was 20-fold higher than that of Spc72N (compare Figure 1d and e).

evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Stu2 localizes to free cMTs in Tub4-depleted cells and that cMT nucleation is abolished when both are depleted.

claim: Stu2 depletion dramatically impaired the formation of cMTs without affecting the assembly of nuclear MTs.
source: Stu2 depletion dramatically impaired the formation of cMTs without affecting the assembly of nuclear MTs (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Stu2 is important for cMT nucleation in vivo in the presence of γ-TuSC.
source: Thus, Stu2 is important for cMT nucleation in vivo in the presence of γ-TuSC.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the Stu2 depletion experiments in TUB4 WT cells.

claim: STU2–AID STU2 cells nucleated SPB-associated cMTs after nocodazole wash out as efficiently as WT STU2 cells.
source: STU2–AID STU2 cells nucleated SPB-associated cMTs after nocodazole wash out (Figure 7e) as efficiently as WT STU2 cells (Figure 7b, WT).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 7e and 7b.

claim: cMTs in STU2–AID STU2 cells were ~1.8 µm long and connected the SPB with the schmoo tip.
source: These cMTs were ~1.8 µm long and connected the SPB with the schmoo tip (Figure 7e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 7e and 7f.

claim: Most stu2TOGAA and stu2∆CC cells were impaired in cMT formation.
source: By contrast, most stu2TOGAA and stu2∆CC cells were impaired in cMT formation (Figure 7e).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Only about 20% of stu2TOGAA and stu2∆CC cells re-assembled cMTs, which were shorter and much less robust than cMTs in STU2–AID STU2 cells.
source: Only about 20% of stu2TOGAA and stu2∆CC cells re-assembled cMTs, which were shorter and much less robust than cMTs in STU2–AID STU2 cells (Figure 7e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 7e and 7f.

claim: About half of the stu2∆MT and stu2∆C cells assembled cMTs that were shorter than those of STU2 WT cells.
source: About half of the stu2∆MT and stu2∆C cells assembled cMTs that were shorter than those of STU2 WT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The other half of stu2∆MT and stu2∆C cells was devoid of cMTs.
source: The other half of stu2∆MT and stu2∆C cells was devoid of cMTs (Figure 7e, quantification).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Whenever STU2 mutant cells assembled cMTs, these were associated with the SPB.
source: Whenever STU2 mutant cells assembled cMTs, these were associated with the SPB (Figure 7e, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The TOG domains and the dimerizing coiled-coil domain of Stu2 were most important for cMT formation in the presence of γ-TuSC.
source: Thus, the TOG domains and the dimerizing coiled-coil domain of Stu2 were most important for cMT formation in the presence of γ-TuSC.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo experiments with Stu2 mutants.

claim: Stu2MT had an important impact on cMT formation.
source: Stu2MT had an important impact on cMT formation.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo experiments with Stu2∆MT mutant.

claim: Stu2 is important for stabilization of the γ-TuSC oligomer at the minus end of detached cMTs.
source: Taken together, our experiments indicate two in vivo functions for Stu2. (1) Stu2 is important for stabilization of the γ-TuSC oligomer at the minus end of detached cMTs (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experiments showing γ-TuSC dissociation when Stu2 is removed.

claim: Stu2 is crucial for the nucleation of cMTs independently of the presence of γ-TuSC.
source: (2) Stu2 is crucial for the nucleation of cMTs independently of the presence of γ-TuSC (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experiments showing cMT nucleation in Tub4-depleted cells that is dependent on Stu2.

claim: The purified Spc72N–Stu2 complex assembles MTs from α/β-tubulin subunits in the form of asters in the absence of γ-TuSC.
source: Here, we show that the purified Spc72N–Stu2 complex assembles MTs from α/β-tubulin subunits in the form of asters in the absence of γ-TuSC.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro MT nucleation assay data.

claim: The aster-forming activity of Spc72N–Stu2 was strongly dependent on the MT-binding region in Stu2.
source: This aster-forming activity was strongly dependent on the MT-binding region in Stu2.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro MT nucleation assay data with Stu2 mutants.

claim: A Stu2 scaffold that is organized by Spc72N stabilizes a first α/β-tubulin seed through its MT-binding site.
source: We propose that a Stu2 scaffold that is organized by Spc72N stabilizes a first α/β-tubulin seed through its MT-binding site, in accordance with the strict requirement for this domain in Spc72N–Stu2-dependent MT nucleation (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: Dimerization of Stu2 is probably important for the nucleation reaction as the Spc72N–Stu2∆CC complex lacked MT nucleation activity.
source: Dimerization of Stu2 is probably important for this nucleation reaction as the Spc72N–Stu2∆CC complex lacked MT nucleation activity (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that deletion of the coiled-coil domain abolishes MT nucleation activity.

claim: γ-TuSC-independent MT nucleation by Stu2 from unattached kinetochores has been reported.
source: γ-TuSC-independent MT nucleation by Stu2 from unattached kinetochores has been reported (Gandhi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: Nucleation of cMTs in the cytoplasm away from the SPB in Tub4-depleted cells is critically dependent on Stu2.
source: Our data now suggest that nucleation of cMTs in the cytoplasm away from the SPB in Tub4-depleted cells is critically dependent on Stu2.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo experiments showing cMT nucleation in Tub4-depleted cells that is abolished when Stu2 is also depleted.

claim: The absence of Spc72 from ectopic cMTs suggests that another scaffold assembles Stu2 into a MT nucleation competent state for the ectopic cMT nucleation reaction.
source: The absence of Spc72 suggests that another scaffold assembles Stu2 into a MT nucleation competent state for the ectopic cMT nucleation reaction.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that ectopic cMTs lack Spc72.

claim: In WT cells, γ-tubulin-independent cMT nucleation events away from the SPB were rare.
source: In WT cells, γ-tubulin-independent cMT nucleation events away from the SPB were rare
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that ectopic cMT nucleation is only observed when Tub4 is depleted.

claim: The Spc72–γ-TuSC system at the SPB is dominant over the Stu2-driven ectopic cMT nucleation.
source: so we have to assume that the Spc72–γ-TuSC system at the SPB is dominant over the Stu2-driven ectopic cMT nucleation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that ectopic cMT nucleation is rare in WT cells.

claim: The dominance of the Spc72–γ-TuSC system ensures that cMTs are anchored to the SPB with a defined polar orientation.
source: This ensures that cMTs are anchored to the SPB with a defined polar orientation.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the functional significance of the dominance of the Spc72–γ-TuSC system.

claim: The defined polar orientation of cMTs is essential for the function of cMTs in nuclear positioning and for orientation of the mitotic spindle.
source: Such an orientation is essential for the function of cMTs in nuclear positioning and for orientation of the mitotic spindle (Hwang et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about cMT function, supported by citation.

claim: Stu2 binds to γ-TuSC via its MT-binding site.
source: Our in vitro data indicate that Stu2 binds to γ-TuSC (Figure 2d) via its MT-binding site (Wang and Huffaker, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro binding data and cited literature.

claim: Human γ-tubulin binds to the MT-binding site of XMAP215 in vitro.
source: This is in line with the recent observation that human γ-tubulin binds to the MT-binding site of XMAP215 in vitro (Thawani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on a recent study, supported by citation.

claim: The interaction of the C-terminus of Stu2 with Spc72, the binding of Stu2MT to γ-tubulin and the binding of the CM1 of Spc72 to Spc97/Spc98 jointly promote the high-affinity interaction of Spc72–Stu2 and γ-TuSC.
source: We suggest that the interaction of the C-terminus of Stu2 with Spc72 (Usui et al., 2003), the binding of Stu2MT to γ-tubulin and the binding of the CM1 of Spc72 to Spc97/Spc98 (Knop and Schiebel, 1997) jointly promote the high-affinity interaction of Spc72–Stu2 and γ-TuSC that we have observed in MST measurements.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on the binding affinity measurements and cited literature.

claim: Stu2 functions structurally as a clamp that joins Spc72 together with γ-TuSC.
source: We propose that Stu2 functions structurally as a clamp that joins Spc72 together with γ-TuSC.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on the binding data.

claim: The MT polymerization activity of Stu2 is not required for γ-TuSC oligomerization.
source: Spc72N–Stu2TOGAA showed γ-TuSC oligomerization activity comparable to that of Spc72N–Stu2WT, suggesting that the MT polymerization activity of Stu2 is not required for γ-TuSC oligomerization.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the gel filtration data comparing Spc72N–Stu2WT and Spc72N–Stu2TOGAA.

claim: The addition of γ-TuSC increased the in vitro MT nucleation activity of Spc72N–Stu2 by a factor of about 3.
source: The addition of γ-TuSC increased the in vitro MT nucleation activity of Spc72N–Stu2 by a factor of about 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro MT nucleation assay data.

claim: The increase in MT nucleation activity is explained by the ability of the γ-tubulin ring to sustain less favoured lateral interactions of α/β-tubulin subunits.
source: This increase is explained by the ability of the γ-tubulin ring to sustain less favoured lateral interactions of α/β-tubulin subunits.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on established knowledge about γ-tubulin function.

claim: The two TOG domains in Stu2 probably promote the recruitment of the first α/β-tubulin subunits to the γ-TuSC template.
source: The two TOG domains in Stu2 probably promote the recruitment of the first α/β-tubulin subunits to the γ-TuSC template.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data showing reduced MT density in asters formed by Spc72N–Stu2TOGAA-γ-TuSC.

claim: The orientation of Stu2 in the Spc72–Stu2–γ-TuSC complex is predetermined by the interaction of its C-terminus with the N-terminally located binding site in Spc72.
source: As the orientation of Stu2 in such a complex is predetermined by the interaction of its C-terminus with the N-terminally located binding site in Spc72 (Usui et al., 2003), each TOG domain orients the α-tubulin subunit of tubulin towards a γ-tubulin molecule in the γ-TuSC oligomer (Ayaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the known binding sites and cited literature.

claim: Each TOG domain orients the α-tubulin subunit of tubulin towards a γ-tubulin molecule in the γ-TuSC oligomer.
source: As the orientation of Stu2 in such a complex is predetermined by the interaction of its C-terminus with the N-terminally located binding site in Spc72 (Usui et al., 2003), each TOG domain orients the α-tubulin subunit of tubulin towards a γ-tubulin molecule in the γ-TuSC oligomer (Ayaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the known binding sites and cited literature.

source: The in vivo situation is even more complex because at least two proteins, Spc72 and Kar9, recruit Stu2 to the minus end of cMTs.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo localization and depletion experiments.

claim: The recruitment role of Kar9 is consistent with the reported interactions of Kar9 with Stu2 and γ-tubulin Tub4.
source: The recruitment role of Kar9 is consistent with the reported interactions of Kar9 with Stu2 and γ-tubulin Tub4 (Chen et al., 1998; Cuschieri et al., 2006; Moore and Miller, 2007; Usui et al., 2003) (illustrated in Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Stu2 probably binds to Kar9 in the Tub4–Kar9 complex via its C-terminal 33 aa of Stu2.
source: Stu2 probably binds to Kar9 in the Tub4–Kar9 complex via its C-terminal 33 aa of Stu2 (Moore and Miller, 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: The TOG domains in the Kar9–Stu2 layer are most probably positioned more distantly away from the cMT minus end than those within Spc72–Stu2.
source: The TOG domains in the Kar9–Stu2 layer are most probably positioned more distantly away from the cMT minus end than those within Spc72–Stu2 (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the proposed model of Stu2 recruitment.

claim: The two Stu2 layers likely function in a sequential order: Spc72–Stu2 functions to add the first α/β-tubulin subunits and then Kar9–Stu2 adds the next α/β-tubulin molecules.
source: The two Stu2 layers likely function in a sequential order: Spc72–Stu2 functions to add the first α/β-tubulin subunits and then Kar9–Stu2adds the next α/β-tubulin molecules (Figure 8).

source: A single XMAP215 molecule that is bound via its MT-binding site to γ-tubulin has, with five TOG domains, a greater reach to add α/β-tubulin subunits to the growing MT than a single Stu2 layer with only two TOG domains (Widlund et al., 2011).

source: Binding of Stu2 to Spc72 and Kar9 probably compensates for the smaller number of TOG domains in Stu2.
